title: The sounds of French
topic: nasal vowels; u vs ou; the French r; silent final letters; liaison and elision
why: A pronunciation lesson built on the words of lessons 1 and 2: nasal vowels, u versus ou, the French r, silent letters, liaison and elision. It gives you the keys to read French aloud correctly and to understand why so many letters stay silent.

Vowels English doesn't have

French spelling looks scary, but it is quite regular once you know a few rules. Let's start with the sounds that don't exist in English.

Nasal vowels

In a nasal vowel, the air goes through the nose and mouth at the same time, and the n or m is not pronounced as a consonant: it only colors the vowel. There are three main ones:

spellingsoundexamples
an, en, am, ema deep “ah” through the noseFrance, enfant, anglais
on, oma round “oh” through the nosebonjour, non, nous avons
in, ain, un, iena flat “a” (as in “bag”) through the nosevin, pain, un, canadien

As soon as a vowel or a second n or m follows, the nasal disappears and you hear a real n: bon / bonne, américain / américaine, canadien / canadienne, un / une. So the feminine of a nationality is not just a spelling change: it sounds different.

u and ou

ou is easy: it's the “oo” of “food”: tout (all), vous, bonjour. But u is a sound English doesn't have: say “ee” and, without moving your tongue, round your lips as for a kiss. That's tu, rue (street), dessus (on top). Practice the pairs: tu / tout, rue / roue (wheel), dessus / dessous (underneath).

é, è and e

é is a short, closed “ay” with no glide: été, étudiant. è and ê are open, as in “bed”: mère, vous êtes. A plain e at the end of a short word is a soft “uh”: le, je, ne.

The French r is made in the throat, a little like gargling softly, not with the tip of the tongue: Paris, rue, bonjour. Try saying “k” and letting air rub at the back of your mouth.

", "

Silent letters

French writes many letters it doesn't pronounce, especially at the end of words. Most final consonants are silent: petit, Paris, vous, les, beaucoup, il est. The plural -s is silent too, and so is the -ent of ils parlent, as you saw in lesson 2.

The CaReFuL rule

Four final consonants are usually pronounced: the letters of the word CaReFuL, c, r, f and l.

letterpronouncedcareful!
cavec, le sacle tabac (c silent)
rbonjour, le professeurthe -er of verbs and many nouns: parler, le dîner sound like “é”
fneuf, actifla clef (an old spelling of la clé)
lil, elle, Michelgentil (l silent)

A final -e with no accent is silent too: la clé ends in “ay”, but la musique ends on the k sound. That's precisely why anglaise makes the s heard: the -e “protects” the consonant before it.

The silent h

The h is never pronounced in French. In most words, it's as if the word began with a vowel: l'hôtel, j'habite, les‿hôtels.

Stress: at the end

English stresses one syllable per word (“HOtel”, “aMErican”). French gives every syllable the same weight and adds a slight stress on the last syllable of a group of words: hô-TEL, a-mé-ri-CAIN, je suis an-GLAIS. Keep your voice even, and lean on the end.

When in doubt, don't pronounce a final consonant: you'll be right far more often than wrong.

", "

Linking words: liaison and elision

French glues words together. A silent final consonant can come back to life when the next word starts with a vowel or a silent h: that's liaison. An s or x then sounds like “z”, a d like “t”, and n links as n.

liaisonexamples
requiredles‿amis, vous‿êtes, nous‿avons, un‿ami, ils‿habitent
forbidden after etun livre et / un stylo
forbidden before an h aspiréles / héros (heroes), le héros, never “l'héros”

An h aspiré is still silent, but it acts like a wall: no liaison and no elision. Dictionaries mark these words, often with an asterisk.

Les‿enfants‿arrivent à l'hôtel.The children arrive at the hotel.

Elision

Some short words lose their vowel before a vowel or a silent h and take an apostrophe. This one is written, so it is never optional:

  • le, la → l': l'ami, l'école, l'hôtel
  • je → j': j'ai, j'habite
  • ne → n': je n'aime pas
  • de → d': un livre d'anglais
Je n'habite pas à l'hôtel, j'ai un ami à Lille.I don't live at the hotel, I have a friend in Lille.

Liaison is why ils‿ont (they have, with a “z”) and ils sont (they are, with an “s”) never sound the same. Say them aloud ten times: it's the best pronunciation drill of the unit.
